title: A Year Ago, India and Canada Were Expelling Each Other's Diplomats. Now Modi Has Been Invited to Ottawa.
excerpt: Four meetings in under a year, a defence dialogue, a $2.6 billion uranium deal, and a trade target of $50 billion by 2030 — the India-Canada reset is moving at a pace that would have been unthinkable during the Khalistan crisis.
body:
In June 2023, Canada and India were pulling their diplomats out of each other's capitals. By June 2026, their prime ministers have met four times in under a year, launched a defence dialogue, signed a uranium supply deal, and set a trade target that would more than double the current volume. The turnaround is not just diplomatic theatre — it has real consequences for the 1.8 million Indians living in Canada.

The latest meeting came on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Evian, France, on June 16. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reviewed what the Ministry of External Affairs called "positive momentum" in relations — a phrase that would have drawn laughs 18 months ago.

## From Expulsions to Energy Deals

The backdrop matters. In September 2023, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau accused India of involvement in the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a Canadian citizen tied to the Khalistan separatist movement, in British Columbia. India denied the allegations. Both countries expelled senior diplomats, froze trade talks, and suspended visa services. For ordinary Indians in Canada — students, professionals, families — the chill was personal. Consular delays spiked, and anti-India rhetoric in Canadian political discourse left many diaspora members feeling exposed.

Carney, who took office last year, moved to bury the crisis with deliberate speed. He kept Punjab off his India itinerary during his first visit in March 2026 — a departure from predecessors who treated the state as a mandatory stop to court Sikh-Canadian voters. The signal was clear: economics first, domestic politics second.

The March visit produced concrete deliverables. India and Canada signed a $2.6 billion uranium supply agreement with Cameco, Canada's mining giant, along with deals on critical minerals and clean energy. A trilateral technology and innovation MoU with Australia followed. Most significantly, the two countries formally launched the India-Canada Defence Dialogue, their first bilateral military engagement mechanism.



> **"India and Canada signed a $2.6 billion uranium supply agreement with Cameco, Canada's mining giant, along with deals on critical minerals and clean energy."**


## What Evian Added

The Evian meeting built on that foundation. Modi and Carney agreed to begin negotiations on a General Security of Information Agreement, or GSOIA — a framework that allows defence contractors and military institutions from both countries to share sensitive information. It is the kind of agreement that underpins joint ventures in defence manufacturing, an area where Canada is pouring billions into modernising its armed forces and India offers industrial manufacturing scale.


![Hardeep Singh Nijjar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/1/19/Photograph_of_the_Canadian_Sikh_activist_Hardeep_Singh_Nijjar.jpg)


Both leaders also announced the establishment of Raisina Americas, a new platform for India-Canada dialogue modelled on India's flagship Raisina Dialogue in New Delhi. India endorsed Canada's bid to join the Indian Ocean Rim Association as a dialogue partner.

On trade, the two sides reaffirmed their target of concluding a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement in 2026 — an ambitious timeline for a deal that would raise bilateral trade to $50 billion by 2030, more than double current levels. Canadian pension funds have already invested $73 billion in India, and the CEPA is designed to open the door wider.

## The Defence Dimension

Canada's High Commissioner to India recently described the relationship as having entered a "reliable, process-driven" phase. That is diplomatic speak for something significant: the two countries are now cooperating on fentanyl precursor supply chains, jointly dismantling international scam centres, and aligning on counter-terrorism in ways that were frozen during the Trudeau years.

The defence angle is particularly notable. Canada is in the middle of a historic military spending increase, and its industrial base needs partners who can manufacture at scale. India, which is trying to build an indigenous defence-industrial ecosystem, fits that profile. The GSOIA negotiations, the appointment of Canada's first Defence Attaché to India, and a new Maritime Security Partnership all point to a relationship that is going deeper than photo opportunities.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians in Canada, the reset is more than a geopolitical headline. During the 2023-24 crisis, consular services slowed, visa processing times ballooned, and the atmosphere in cities like Brampton and Surrey grew uncomfortable. Community leaders reported an uptick in anti-India sentiment, often conflating the actions of the Indian state with ordinary diaspora members.

The Carney government has been careful to separate the security dialogue — which includes ongoing law enforcement cooperation on the Nijjar case — from the broader relationship. A new MoU between India's AICTE and Canada's Mitacs will fund 300 research internships annually for Indian students starting in 2027, a tangible signal that the people-to-people pipeline is being rebuilt.

Modi accepted Carney's invitation to visit Canada later this year. If it happens, it will be the first bilateral visit by an Indian prime minister to Canada since 2018. For the diaspora, that visit will matter less for what it produces than for what it symbolises: that the two countries have moved past the worst chapter in their modern relationship, and that 1.8 million Indians in Canada are no longer caught in the crossfire.
